extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent attorneys/practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and arguing novelty/obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. §§102 and 103, including inherency, product/composition/process distinctions, product-by-process and apparatus claim treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on express, implicit, and inherent disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: The express, implicit, and inherent disclosures of a prior art reference may be relied upon in the rejection of claims under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inherency is a question of fact and may establish anticipation or obviousness (e.g., In re Napier, In re Grasselli). Examiner may rely on what is expressly disclosed, what is implicit, and what is inherently taught by the prior art reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of new property does not make old composition patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery of a previously unappreciated property of a prior art composition, or of a scientific explanation for the prior art’s functioning, does not render the old composition patentably new to the discoverer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claiming a new use, function, or unknown property which is inherently present in the prior art does not necessarily make the claim patentable (Atlas Powder Co. v. IRECO; In re Best; In re Crish). See MPEP § 2112.01 re inherency and product-by-process claims and § 2141.02 re inherency and 103 rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent feature need not be recognized at time of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no requirement that a person of ordinary skill in the art would have recognized the inherent disclosure at the time of invention; only that the subject matter is in fact inherent in the prior art reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts hold that an inherent structure, composition, or function need not have been known or recognized in the prior art at the time (Schering Corp. v. Geneva Pharm.; Toro Co. v. Deere & Co.; Abbott Labs v. Geneva Pharms.; SmithKline Beecham). Post‑critical date evidence or expert testimony may be considered to show inherency if the characteristic necessarily flows from prior art teachings.

rubrics_metrics.name: 102/103 rejection appropriate when prior art product appears identical but silent on characteristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Where applicant claims a composition in terms of a function, property, or characteristic and the composition of the prior art is the same as that of the claim but the function is not explicitly disclosed by the reference, the examiner may make a rejection under both 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (a 102/103 rejection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is nothing inconsistent in asserting anticipation under 102 and obviousness under 103 concurrently (In re Best). This applies to product, apparatus, and process claims claimed in terms of function/property/characteristic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must provide rationale/evidence supporting inherency
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that a certain result or characteristic may occur or be present in the prior art is not sufficient; the examiner must provide a basis in fact and/or technical reasoning to reasonably support the determination that the characteristic necessarily flows from the applied prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections based on conjecture or on an invitation to investigate are improper (In re Rijckaert; In re Oelrich; Metabolite Labs.). Ex parte Levy: examiner must provide objective evidence or cogent technical reasoning. Examples: Board reversed where examiner failed to provide objective evidence that a balloon was biaxially oriented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden shifts to applicant once examiner shows inherency
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a reference teaching a product appearing to be substantially identical is made the basis of a rejection, and the examiner presents evidence or reasoning tending to show inherency, the burden of production shifts to the applicant to show the prior art products do not necessarily or inherently possess the characteristics of the claimed product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must provide objective evidence (e.g., experimental comparisons, declarations with relevant measured dimensions or data) to rebut the prima facie case. Cases: In re Best; In re Fitzgerald; In re Schreiber; MPEP § 2112.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product/apparatus claims: identical or substantially identical structure presumes properties/functions inherent
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the claimed and prior art products are identical or substantially identical in structure or composition, or are produced by identical or substantially identical processes, a prima facie case of either anticipation or obviousness has been established and claimed properties/functions are presumed inherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the PTO shows a sound basis for believing the products are the same, applicant has burden to show they are not (In re Best; In re Spada; Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner). Applicant can rebut by showing the prior art product does not necessarily possess the claimed characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition claims: identical chemical structure implies same properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Products of identical chemical composition cannot have mutually exclusive properties; if the prior art teaches the identical chemical structure, the properties applicant discloses and/or claims are necessarily present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtual identity of monomers and procedures can support prima facie unpatentability for lack of novelty (In re Spada). Applicant must produce evidence to show a real difference in properties if asserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonfunctional printed matter does not distinguish product claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the only difference between a prior art product and a claimed product is printed matter that is not functionally related to the product, the printed matter will not distinguish the claimed product from the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical inquiry is whether there exists any new and unobvious functional relationship between the printed matter and the substrate (In re Ngai; In re Gulack; In re Miller). Courts extend this to 'instruction limitations' in method claims—informational limitations that do not transform or depend on the method are non-functional (King Pharmaceuticals v. Eon Labs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims: prior art device anticipates a claimed process if device inherently carries out the process during normal operation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior art device, in its normal and usual operation, would necessarily perform the method claimed, then the method claimed will be considered to be anticipated by the prior art device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the prior art device is the same as a device described in the specification for carrying out the claimed method, it can be assumed the device will inherently perform the claimed process. Applicant must present evidence (e.g., comparative data) to rebut (In re King; In re Best; Ex parte Novitski).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process-of-use claims: new uses of old structures may be patentable, but claims directed to mere discovery of a property are anticipated
rubrics_metrics.description: A discovery of a new use for an old structure may be patentable as a process of using; however, when the claim recites using an old composition/structure and the 'use' is directed to a result or property of that composition/structure, the claim is anticipated if the prior art already reads on that property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding a new property of an old compound does not necessarily create a patentable new use (In re Hack; In re May; In re Tomlinson). Distinguish true new uses from mere recognition of previously inherent properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims judged on the product, not the process
rubrics_metrics.description: Even though product-by-process claims are limited by the recited process, determination of patentability is based on the product itself; if the product is the same as or obvious from a prior art product, the claim is unpatentable even if the prior product was made by a different process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement analysis differs (infringement only by product made by recited process), but validity is determined by product identity (In re Thorpe; Amgen v. F. Hoffmann‑La Roche). Consider structure implied by process steps when assessing patentability (In re Garnero).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden shifts to applicant for product-by-process claims when prior art appears identical
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a product appearing to be the same or only slightly different from the claimed product is shown and a 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejection is made, the burden shifts to the applicant to come forward with evidence establishing an unobvious difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO bears a lesser burden in making a prima facie obviousness case for product-by-process claims; applicants should present comparison data or evidence of unexpected properties to rebut (In re Fessmann; In re Marosi; Ex parte Gray).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejections for product-by-process claims is acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: When the prior art discloses a product which reasonably appears to be identical with or only slightly different from a product claimed in a product-by-process claim, a rejection based alternatively on either section 102 or section 103 is fair and acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must explain both anticipation and obviousness aspects of such rejections; practical limits on Office ability to physically compare many products support this approach (In re Brown).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus claims: inherency and functional limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: If an examiner concludes that a functional limitation is an inherent characteristic of the prior art, the examiner should explain that the prior art structure inherently possesses the limitations of the claimed apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burden shifts to applicant to show prior art does not possess the relied-on characteristic (In re Schreiber; Bettcher Industries v. Bunzl; In re Swinehart). See MPEP §§2173.05(g), 2181–2186 for means-plus-function guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of operating device does not differentiate apparatus claims from prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: An apparatus claim covers what a device is, not what a device does; a recitation regarding intended use or manner of operation does not differentiate the claimed apparatus from prior art if the prior art teaches all the structural limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble use or specified intended employment is immaterial to structure-based rejections (Hewlett‑Packard Co. v. Bausch & Lomb; Ex parte Masham). Examiners should focus on structural limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural differences can prevent anticipation even if prior art performs same functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the prior art device performs all the functions recited in the claim, the prior art cannot anticipate the claim if there is any structural difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means‑plus‑function limitations are met by structures equivalent to corresponding structures in the specification; claims may require specific structural elements (In re Donaldson; In re Robertson). Examiner should analyze structural correspondence, not solely functional equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claim language without structural limitation covers all devices capable of performing the function
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional claim language that is not limited to a specific structure covers all devices that are capable of performing the recited function, affecting the scope of what is anticipated or obvious under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is functional-only (no structure), it may be read broadly to cover any device performing the function; examiners should consider whether the claim needs structural limitation or whether prior art devices inherently fall within such broad functional language. (Section introduces treatment for computer‑implemented functional claim limitations.)
